food.text: Egypt was one of the first areas to adopt the Neolithic package, a set of farming practices that came from West Asia as early as the 6th millennium BCE. Goats and sheep, which are not indigenous to Africa, arrived from the Neolithic Levant around 6000 BCE, probably through the Sinai Peninsula. They then spread rapidly.

Long before the pharaohs, the people of the Nile valley and Delta were self-sufficient farmers. They raised barley and emmer, an early variety of wheat, and stored the grain in pits lined with reed mats. They also raised cattle, goats and pigs.

By the eighth millennium BCE, a Neolithic culture in what is now Sudan had settled into fortified mudbrick villages. There, people supplemented hunting and fishing on the Nile with grain gathering and cattle herding.

From about 5000 to 4200 BC, the Merimde culture flourished at a large settlement at the edge of the Western Delta. Its people kept cattle, sheep, goats and pigs, and planted wheat, sorghum and barley. The culture had strong connections to the Faiyum A culture as well as the Levant.

Studies of morphological, genetic and archaeological data attribute the Neolithic settlements that appeared across Egypt around 6000 BC to migrants from the Fertile Crescent. These migrants returned during the Neolithic Revolution and brought agriculture to the region.

As natural climate changes around the 8th millennium BC began to dry out the extensive pastoral lands of North Africa, the early ancestors of the Egyptians were forced to settle around the Nile more permanently. This pushed them toward a more sedentary lifestyle.

During the fifth millennium BC, migrations from the drying Sahara brought Neolithic people into the Nile Valley, along with agriculture. The mixing of these newcomers with the existing population later developed into a social hierarchy that became the Kingdom of Kerma at 2500 BC.

The oldest-known domesticated cattle remains in Africa come from the Faiyum, dated to c. 4400 BC. Evidence of cattle herding near the Sudan border before the 8th millennium BC exists, but an independent domestication of cattle in Africa must be abandoned, because thirty years of later evidence has failed to support it.

art.text: Ancient Egyptian art covers a huge span of time, starting in the 6th millennium BC and lasting until the 4th century AD. It included paintings, sculptures, faience, jewelry, ivories and architecture. Its style changed very little over that time.
The ancient Egyptian language had no word for "art". Artworks served a functional purpose bound up with religion and ideology, and to render a subject in art was to grant it permanence.

During the predynastic period, relief and painting were inseparable. In most cases the artist used both the brush and the chisel to create a work, and the main purpose of painting was to enhance the sculpture with colours.
Naqada II pottery, made from about 3500 to 3200 BC, was painted mostly in dark red. It showed animals, people and ships, along with geometric symbols that appear to have been derived from animals.

The Tasian culture, which existed in Upper Egypt starting about 4500 BC, is notable for producing the earliest blacktop-ware. This was a type of red and brown pottery painted black on its top and interior.
Around 3500 BC the Early A-Group culture arose in Lower Nubia. During this time the Nubians began creating distinctive black-topped, red pottery.

Naqada II pottery is distinctly different from the earlier Naqada I white cross-lined wares or black-topped ware. Its wavy handles, rare before this period, became more common and more elaborate until they were almost completely ornamental.

The Badarian culture, from about 4400 to 4000 BC, continued to produce blacktop-ware pottery, though much improved in quality. Unlike the Neolithic Tasian sites, Badarian sites also used copper alongside stone, making them chalcolithic settlements.

A-Group Nubians traded with the Egyptians and exported gold. Their graves held Egyptian imports such as gold objects, faience amulets and beads, seals, slate palettes, stone vessels and a variety of pots.

Around 3100 BC, the wealth of A-group kings rivaled that of Egyptian kings, and royal A-group graves contained gold and richly decorated pottery. Some scholars believe Nubian A-Group rulers and early Egyptian pharaohs used related royal symbols, a view supported by similarities in A-Group Nubia and Upper Egypt rock art.

Some Naqada I paintings depict a triumphant warrior with his captives, a likely prototype of later scenes of pharaohs smiting their enemies. On Jar E3002, dated to Naqada IC-IIA (c. 3800-3600 BC), two tall victors with raised arms stand over smaller, apparently arm-less figures, four of whom are attached to the central victor with ropes at their necks. These scenes of warfare in the Nile Valley may be a prelude to the later scenes of pharaohs smiting their enemies.

Wavy-line pottery developed six ceramic subvariants, while dotted wavy-line pottery developed three. The earliest development of both, in the 8th millennium BCE, took place at Sagai and Sarurab in Sudan.
University of Chicago Oriental Institute scholars excavated at Qustul, near Abu Simbel in Sudan, in 1960 to 1964. They found artifacts that incorporated images associated with Egyptian pharaohs.

The earliest known representations of pharaonic iconography were excavated at Nag el-Hamdulab in Aswan, in the far south of Egypt near the Sudan border. They are estimated to date between 3200 and 3100 BC.

Wavy-line pottery turned up at many sites across Africa, including the Hoggar Mountains in southern Algeria, Tibesti in Chad and Adrar Madet in Niger. Most finds, however, are in the Central Nile region.

war.text: A carved sandstone relief from the Second Cataract, dated to around 3000 BCE, possibly describes a war between the Egyptians and the A-Group Nubian people. It shows the victory of an Egyptian king.

One proposal dates the Gebel Sheikh Suleiman relief to the pharaoh Djer or Djet. Djet was the third king of the First Dynasty and is known for his victorious expeditions to Nubia. If so, the relief may commemorate a real royal campaign south along the Nile.

The relief shows the victor as a serekh, a royal emblem, although the serekh gives no specific royal name. A boat is considered an embodiment of the king, dominating defeated Nubians. Circles at the bottom of the scene represent cities.

The relief is carved on a large sandstone block measuring 2.75 by 0.80 metres. It is an early example of low relief carving. Its symbolism and early hieroglyphic markings point to the First Dynasty or Second Dynasty of Egypt.

The relief comes from the Second Cataract, just south of Buhen, one of the most ancient frontiers in the history of mankind. In 1963 it was moved to the National Museum of Sudan in Khartoum. This was done before the area was drowned by the water of Lake Nasser.

The victory imagery of the relief resembles the earlier Gebel el-Arak Knife and the fresco from Tomb 100 at Hierakonpolis, both from the Naqada II period. It might be a slight archaism, meant to legitimize the rule of the early pharaoh who commissioned it.

science.text: In the 5th millennium BCE, people built stone circles at Nabta Playa that may have made use of astronomical alignments. Egyptian astronomy is thought to reach back to this prehistoric period, well before the Dynastic Period began.

Geological evidence and computer climate modeling suggest that natural climate changes around the 8th millennium BC began to dry out the extensive pastoral lands of North Africa. Between 5500 BC and the 31st century BC, small settlements flourished along the Nile.

The stone circles at Nabta Playa lie in Lower Nubia, inside the borders of modern Egypt but south of the border of Ancient Egypt. Dating from the 5th millennium BCE, they suggest astronomy was important to the religious life of prehistoric people near ancient Egypt.

The oldest known domesticated cattle remains in Africa come from the Faiyum and date to about 4400 BC. Evidence of cattle herding near the Sudan border before the 8th millennium BC did not hold up, so an independent African domestication of cattle has been abandoned.

The Badarian culture, from about 4400 to 4000 BC, used copper in addition to stone, so its sites are considered chalcolithic. The earlier Tasian sites, though very similar, are still counted as Stone Age. This copper use is the main difference that keeps scholars from merging the two periods.

Neolithic settlements in central Nubia date back to 7000 BC, and Wadi Halfa is believed to be the oldest settlement in the central Nile valley. By about 6000 BC, peoples in the region had developed an agricultural economy.

Population genetics in the Nile Valley show a marked change around 6000 BCE, visible in odontometric and dental tissue changes. This coincides with the arrival of the Neolithic package from West Asia, with its farmed animals and crops.

Archaeologists gave pottery styles sequence dating (SD) numbers to order them in time. Badarian pottery was assigned SD 21 to 29, while Naqada II pottery, from about 3500 to 3200 BC, has SD values of 40 through 62.

Cultural exchange between Egypt and Mesopotamia continued through the 4th millennium BCE. It is shown by the transfer of Mesopotamian Late Uruk period features to the Nile Valley in the later Predynastic Period.

politics.text: Egypt's historical records begin with a unified state, which arose around 3150 BC. According to Egyptian tradition, Menes, thought to have joined Upper and Lower Egypt, was the first king.

Before unification, the land of Egypt was settled with autonomous villages. Afterward the country came to be known as "The Two Lands", meaning Upper and Lower Egypt. The pharaohs set up a national administration and appointed royal governors.

The end of Predynastic Egypt is disputed, because finds show a gradual development rather than a sharp break. Scholars use terms like "Protodynastic period", "Zero Dynasty" or "Dynasty 0" for the stretch that some call Predynastic and others Early Dynastic.

During Naqada III, the names of kings were inscribed as serekhs on a variety of surfaces, including pottery and tombs. The kings headed powerful polities, and the later part of the period is associated with Dynasty 0.

Egyptian settlement and colonization are attested from about 3200 BC across southern Canaan. Twenty serekhs attributed to Narmer, the first ruler of the Early Dynastic Period, have been found there. The colony was likely run from Tell es-Sakan, a fortified settlement inhabited from 3300 to 3000 BC.

A sandstone relief from the Second Cataract, just south of Buhen, possibly shows a war between Egyptians and the A-Group Nubian people. It shows the victory of an Egyptian king, represented by his serekh, and has been proposed to date to Djer or Djet of the First Dynasty.

No detailed records of the first two dynasties survive, apart from the terse lists on the Palermo Stone. What we know comes from a few monuments bearing royal names, chiefly the Narmer Palette and Narmer Macehead.

Manetho's Aegyptiaca names nine rulers of the First Dynasty, but only one name matches the other sources, and he gives information on just four. His account contradicts both the archeological evidence and the other historical records.

Christopher Ehret states that retainer sacrifice, the burial of human retainers killed to accompany a pharaoh, found in the first dynastic royal tombs of Abydos, originated in the southern Middle Nile region. He adds that the ritual practice was shared with the Kerma kingdom of the Upper Nubian Nile. In the First Dynasty, retainers were buried near each pharaoh's tomb, along with sacrificed animals, and the tomb of Djer is associated with the burials of 338 individuals.

Early Egyptian kings held as many as three titles: the Horus name, the Sedge and Bee name, and the Two Ladies or Nebty name. The earliest Nebty name comes from king Aha and links the king with the goddesses Nekhbet and Wadjet, patrons of Upper and Lower Egypt.
A second inscription found near the relief shows a large scorpion with bound captives. It seems to date from slightly earlier and is possibly related to king Scorpion II.

culture.text: The A-Group was the first powerful society in Nubia, flourishing between the First and Second Cataracts of the Nile. Its people lived mostly in reed huts and rock shelters, and most settlements were temporary or pastoralist communities. They were semi-nomadic herders who also fished, hunted and gathered.

Goats and sheep are not native to Africa. They were introduced to Egypt from the Neolithic Levant around 6000 BCE, probably through the Sinai Peninsula, and then spread rapidly. They were part of the Neolithic package that reached Egypt from West Asia.

Predynastic Egyptian potters made red-bodied, black-topped vessels. The red came naturally from firing Nilotic clay rich in ferrous oxide, while the black top was made by exposing the top of the vessel to dense black soot. The style began in the Badarian culture and was still made throughout the Naqada period.

In the Merimde culture of the western Nile Delta, the dead were not buried in separate cemeteries. They were laid in a flexed position in oval pits inside the settlement, without grave goods or offerings. This differed from burial customs in Upper Egyptian Predynastic Egypt.

Around 3500 BC the Early A-Group culture arose in Lower Nubia. A-Group Nubians were semi-nomadic herders and rudimentary agriculturalists who also fished, hunted and gathered. Evidence of agriculture appears only in the Terminal A-Group period, circa 3200 to 3000 BC.

A-Group burials at Serra East show the dead lying on either side, with the head facing south or east. The bodies were curled up, with hands near the face and legs folded upward. Leather wrappings served as clothing and bags, though these were not typically found in more lavish cemeteries.

Cylinder seals appear suddenly in Egypt around 3500 to 3300 BC, during Naqada II c-d, with no local antecedents. Their designs resemble those of Mesopotamia, where the seals were invented during the Uruk period in the early 4th millennium BC.

Two golden statuettes found at Tell el-Farkha show standing naked men, one 60 cm tall and the other 30 cm, with lapis lazuli eyes, bald heads, large protruding ears and unnaturally large phalluses. Both wear very large phallus sheaths, and one sheath is decorated with a carved band. They most probably depict a Predynastic ruler and his son during the heb-sed festival, and probably adorned a shrine in the Western Kom area. They are thought to date to Naqada IIIB, c. 3200 to 3000 BC, and to be the oldest known depictions of Ancient Egyptian rulers.

Naqada literally means "Golden Town", reflecting the wealth of the Eastern Desert in gold. Naqada and its facing town of Koptos held a strategic position in the commerce of that gold. Together with surplus-producing floodplain agriculture, this helped the region develop specialized crafts.

Around 3500 BC the Early A-Group culture arose in Lower Nubia, made up of semi-nomadic herders who also fished, hunted and gathered. Yet the A-Group also traded with the Egyptians, exporting gold. Large amounts of Egyptian goods, including copper tools, were placed in A-Group graves.

Cemetery L at Qustul holds an elite A-Group burial containing nearly 200 pottery vessels. Some of the vessels held expensive imports from Egypt and Palestine. Decorative vessels were more likely to be found in larger tombs, while simpler burials held ripple-burnished or plain vessels.

The earliest Egyptian cylinder seals are clearly similar to Uruk seals down to Naqada II-d, circa 3300 BC, and may even have been made by Mesopotamian craftsmen. From about 3300 BC they began to diverge and become more Egyptian in character.

A-Group graves in Nubia held large amounts of Egyptian goods, including gold objects, copper tools, faience amulets and beads, seals, slate palettes and stone vessels. During this time the Nubians also began making their own distinctive black-topped, red pottery.
